## Project-oriented workflows

Key takeaways: 

1. Each project should have an **isolated** package environment that preserves the names and versions. 

2. The project's dependencies/requirements should be captured in a way that **makes it exportable/transferable to another machine**.[^renv-venv]

3. Each project should have a **virtual environment** in a **standalone directory** that documents everything the project needs (usually in a GitHub or GitLab repo).[^rstats-wtf-projects]

[^rstats-wtf-projects]: Read more in [What They Forgot to Teach You About R: Chapter 3, Project-oriented workflow](https://rstats.wtf/projects)

[^renv-venv]: In R, this is [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html). In Python, this is [`venv`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment).

## Virtual environments

As [do4ds notes](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html), `venv` and `renv` "*keep user-level package caches of the actual packages and use symlinks, so only one copy of the package is installed.*"

### `renv`

First, read the documentation on [project level management with `renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html) and [using renv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-renv).

I’ve summarized the steps below:

1. Create a new R project-local environment

    ```r
    install.packages("renv")
    renv::init()
    ```

2. Install packages into the renv-managed environment

    ```r
    install.packages(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2"))
    ```

3. Snapshot the state of the environment and package versions in the lock file (`renv.lock`)

    ```r
    renv::snapshot()
    ```

4. To deactivate the environment, restart R or close the session `renv` projects are automatically reactivated the time a project is opened. Restore the environment on a new system with:

    ```r
    renv::restore()
    ```

To demonstrate how to use `renv`, I've copied the `eda-basic.qmd` file into it's own 'project' folder (`renv-eda-basic`):

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/
└── eda-basic.qmd
```

:::

Then I ran `renv::init()`: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::init()
```

```{r}
#| collapse: true
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
fs::dir_tree(
  path = "_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/", 
  all = TRUE, 
  recurse = 1)
```

Initiating `renv` in a project root directory will create the `.Rprofile` and `renv.lock` files and a `renv/` folder:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
_labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/
├── .Rprofile
├── eda-basic.qmd
├── renv/
├── renv-eda-basic.Rproj
└── renv.lock
```

:::

`renv::init()` will also create `renv-eda-basic.Rproj`, which helps enforce project-oriented workflows (but these are specific to RStudio).  

To install the packages, we can use `install.packages()` or `pak::pak()` for more flexible installations:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2"))
```

```{r}
#| label: co_box_renv_install
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "b",
  look = "default", 
  hsize = "1.25", 
  size = "1.00", 
  header = "**Note**", 
  fold = FALSE,
  contents = "`renv::install()` uses cached packages when available. Otherwise, it installs the latest version from CRAN.")
```

Create a snapshot (i.e., the current versions of R and any installed packages, along with the R repositories) with `renv::snapshot()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::snapshot()
```

The dependencies are saved in the `renv.lock` file, which should be committed to version control. 

To make sure the dependencies in the `renv.lock` file have been installed (i.e., after cloning), run: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
renv::restore()
```

The diagram below maps how packages flow between CRAN, the `renv` cache, the project library, and the lockfile:


### `venv`

Read the [documentation on Python virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment) and using [venv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-venv). 

I've summarized the steps below:

1. Create new Python 3 virtual environment in the `.venv` directory 

    ```bash
    python3 -m venv .venv
    ```

2. Activate the environment

    ```bash
    source .venv/bin/activate
    ```

3. Use `pip` to install packages into your environment

    ```bash
    python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas
    ```

4. Deactivate an environment

    ```bash 
    deactivate
    ```

5. Save environment

    ```bash
    python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
    ```

6. Restoring environment

    ```bash 
    python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt
    ```

Use the **Terminal** to navigate to the `venv-model-basic-py` folder and create the Python virtual environment: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
python3 -m venv .venv
```

This will create a `.venv/` folder inside `venv-model-basic-py`.

```{r}
#| collapse: true
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
fs::dir_tree(
  path = "_labs/lab01/venv-model-basic-py/", 
  all = TRUE, 
  recurse = 1)
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
_labs/lab01/venv-model-basic-py/
├── .venv
│   ├── bin
│   ├── include
│   ├── lib
│   └── pyvenv.cfg
└── model-basic-py.qmd
```

:::


To activate the virtual environment, run the following in the **Terminal**:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
source .venv/bin/activate
```

This should change the **Terminal** prompt from: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ 
```

to: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
(.venv) Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$
```

Now we can install required Python packages (we include `jupyter` for interactive outputs) 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
pip install palmerpenguins pandas numpy scikit-learn jupyter
```

To store the installed packages, save them to a `requirements.txt` file with `pip freeze`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

#### Rendering with Python

To render, use the following in the **Terminal**: 

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
quarto preview model-basic-py.qmd --no-browser --no-watch-inputs
```

To tell Quarto to use the virtual environment, we can place the following in the `model-basic-py.qmd` file:

```yaml
execute:
  python: .venv/bin/python
```

Or we can set the Python interpreter with the **Terminal**:[^venv-win]

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
quarto use python .venv/bin/python3
```

[^venv-win]: On Windows try `.venv\Scripts\python.exe`


If you're working inside **RStudio or Posit Workbench**, consider letting `reticulate` manage the Python environment:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("myenv", required = TRUE)
virtualenv_install(
  envname = "myenv", 
  packages = c("palmerpenguins", "pandas", "numpy", 
               "scikit-learn", "jupyter"))
```

This ensures RStudio uses a known-good Python environment.

Now, if we open the `model-basic-py.qmd` file in RStudio and click the **Render** button in the toolbar we should see the rendered output.

## Recap

1. Each project gets its own isolated, transferable package environment. In R, `renv::init()` creates the project library and `renv.lock`, `renv::snapshot()` records the package versions, and `renv::restore()` reinstalls them on another machine.

2. In Python, `python3 -m venv .venv` creates the environment and `source .venv/bin/activate` turns it on. `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures the installed packages, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` restores them.

3. Quarto has to be told which Python interpreter to use. We can add `python: .venv/bin/python` under `execute:` in the document's YAML, run `quarto use python .venv/bin/python3` in the Terminal, or let `reticulate` manage the environment inside RStudio.

Next, [Modeling in Python](model-basic-py.qmd) walks through the code in `model-basic-py.qmd`.
